publication_scope.blurb: Ludwig Crocius — Book I Chapter 8 On Sacred Scripture's efficacy, from the 1636 Bremen Latin. Densify COMPLETE (PHYS mid-276–mid-290): efficacy defined as Scripture's property of illuminating and vivifying by the Spirit's elevated instrument; differs from mere perspicuity; objective and effective efficacy; letter alone does not convert; prior grace-light required; Scripture reading for all; against papal vernacular bans, intermittent reading, laity bans, and hanging-Scripture superstition. Cap. 8 On Scripture's efficacy begins mid PHYS 276; Cap. 6 complete; the rest of the Syntagma remains.

source_text: CAPUT OCTAVUM. De sacrae Scripturae efficacia. Haec de sacrae Scripturae interpretatione: Efficacia est illius proprietas, qua apta nata est hominem Dei decenter audientem aut legentem per modum instrumenti ac luminis a Spiritu sancto accensi & elevati illuminare, movere, mortificare, vivificare ac perficere, ut ad omne bonum opus perfecte instructus sit. Apostoli hanc verbi Dei proprietatem magnifice extollunt, Rom. 1.v.16. Hebr. 4.v.12. 2. Cor. 3.v.6. 2. Petri 1.v.19. 2. Tim. 3.v.16.17. fluentem a Spiritu sancto, ut causa principe illud tanquam organum sua virtute elevante, Joh. 6.v.63. 1. Petri 1. ubi & sub finem capitis semen immortale dicitur: qui spiritus interficit spiritum impurum, vincit malum, e medio tollit Antichristum, renovat omnia sub coelo, liberat creaturam a peccato, vanitate, maledictione, illuminat luce sua tenebras nostras & implet terram cognitione Dei, Zach. 13.v.2. Apoc. 12.v.11. 1. Thess. 2.v.13. Esa. 11.v.4. Joel 2.v.28. Ezech. 36.v.25. Esa. 32.v.15. Rom. 8.v.21. Apoc. 18.v.1. Esa. 11.v.9. Haec efficacia differt a perspicuitate sacrae Scripturae, qua efficitur, ut non solum homines sanae mentis, sed & cacodaemones sensus illius cognitu ad salutem necessarios, sine interna Spiritus sancti illuminatione, clare intelligant, etsi eos credere, eisque obedire nequeant, sed fidem & obsequium dissuadeant. Videas Whitakerum cap. 1. de Scripturae perspicuitate & D. Festum Hommium disp. 62. de fide thes. 5.
english:
CHAPTER EIGHT
On Sacred Scripture's efficacy

So far concerning Sacred Scripture's interpretation: Efficacy is its property by which it is apt by nature to illuminate, move, mortify, vivify, and perfect the man of God who hears or reads decently, by way of an instrument and of a light kindled and elevated by the Holy Spirit — so that he is thoroughly equipped for every good work.

The Apostles magnificently exalt this property of God's word ([[Romans 1:16 >> Bible:Romans 1:16]]; [[Hebrews 4:12 >> Bible:Hebrews 4:12]]; [[2 Corinthians 3:6 >> Bible:2 Corinthians 3:6]]; [[2 Peter 1:19 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:19]]; [[2 Timothy 3:16 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:16]]–[[2 Timothy 3:17 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:17]]) — a property flowing from the Holy Spirit as principal cause, elevating that word as its organ by its own power ([[John 6:63 >> Bible:John 6:63]]; [[1 Peter 1:23 >> Bible:1 Peter 1:23]], where toward the chapter's end it is also called immortal seed). That Spirit kills the impure spirit, conquers evil, removes Antichrist from the midst, renews all things under heaven, frees the creature from sin, vanity, and curse, illuminates our darkness with its light, and fills the earth with the knowledge of God ([[Zechariah 13:2 >> Bible:Zechariah 13:2]]; [[Revelation 12:11 >> Bible:Revelation 12:11]]; [[1 Thessalonians 2:13 >> Bible:1 Thessalonians 2:13]]; [[Isaiah 11:4 >> Bible:Isaiah 11:4]]; [[Joel 2:28 >> Bible:Joel 2:28]]; [[Ezekiel 36:25 >> Bible:Ezekiel 36:25]]; [[Isaiah 32:15 >> Bible:Isaiah 32:15]]; [[Romans 8:21 >> Bible:Romans 8:21]]; [[Revelation 18:1 >> Bible:Revelation 18:1]]; [[Isaiah 11:9 >> Bible:Isaiah 11:9]]).

This efficacy differs from Sacred Scripture's perspicuity, by which it comes about that not only people of sound mind but even evil spirits clearly understand those senses of it needful to know for salvation — without the Holy Spirit's inward illumination — even though they cannot believe or obey them, but rather dissuade faith and obedience. See Whitaker, chapter 1 On Scripture's perspicuity, and Dr. Festus Hommius, Disputation 62 On faith, thesis 5.

source_text: 4. Errare omnium gravissime, qui lectionem Biblicam laicis, quos vocant, interdicunt. Haec enim tyrannis in papatu exercetur. Nam Joh. Azorius Jesuita tom. 1. moral. instit. lib. 8. cap. 26. Quaeris, inquit, an Bibliorum libri & capita in vulgari lingua translata permittantur? Resp. primo adspectu in quarta regula prohibiti sunt, ne sc. Biblia vulgari lingua passim sine discrimine permittantur legi. In Hispania tamen in indice librorum prohibitorum ibi edito auctoritate generalis inquisitoris regula sexta sic habet: Prohibentur Biblia in vulgari lingua cum omnibus suis partibus. Et in indice recenti edito jussu Clementis octavi pontificis, sublata est facultas concedendi licentiam legendi vel retinendi Biblia vulgaria aut alias sacrae Scripturae tam Novi quam V. Testamenti partes, quamvis vulgari lingua editas. Idem cum aliis sentit Thomas Hardingus contra Juellum Art. 15. sect. 2. apud Johan. Juellum tom. 1. p. 120. Renatus Benedictus Andegavus lib. 3. Stromat. Biblic. p. 177. Joh. Bunderius in compendio rerum Theologiae tit. 3. art. 3. Joh. Molanus Lovan. in compendio Theologiae practicae tract. 3. cap. 23. conclus. 2. pag. 221. 5. Errare, qui sacras Scripturas e collo suspensas variis virtutibus contra mundi pericula, morbos, daemones, praeditas credunt. Hunc Romanae ecclesiae morem Alfonsus Salmeron tom. 4. comment. in hist. Euang. part. 3. tract. 42. simpliciter improbare non audet, ut & Martinus Delrio lib. 1. disquis. magic. cap. 4. quaest. 4. Joh. Maldonatus in Johan. 6. Vitus Miletus in discuss. 600. errorum pag. 51. 52. Landulfus Carthusiensis in meditationibus vitae Christi parte 2. cap. 63. Verbum, inquit, CONSUMMATUM, magnae efficaciae esse in periculis perhibetur ab expertis. Et specialiter valere dicitur in immoderatum fluxum sanguinis de naribus, si cum eodem sanguine scribatur idem verbum in fronte patientis. Alia exempla pontificiae superstitionis notavit Joh. Wierus lib. 5. de praestigiis daemonum cap. 4. & Mart. Delrio lib. 3. disquis. mag. parte 2. quaest. 4. sect. 9. Huc refer Enchiridion Manualeve, quo habentur oratio devota Leonis papae, aliquot item orationes adversus omnia mundi pericula, oratio B. Augustini & Cypriani, Venetiis apud Thomam Membrunium editum; ex quo clare perspicietur, quam malitiose abutatur pontificia Romana ecclesia verbis Scripturae ad superstitionem & magiam.
english: 4. That those err most gravely of all who forbid biblical reading to those they call laity. For this tyranny is exercised in the papacy. For the Jesuit Juan Azor, Moral Institutions volume 1 book 8 chapter 26: "You ask," he says, "whether the books and chapters of the Bible translated into the vulgar tongue are permitted? Answer: at first glance they are forbidden in the fourth rule, namely that Bibles in the vulgar tongue not be permitted to be read everywhere without distinction. Yet in Spain, in the index of prohibited books published there by the General Inquisitor's authority, the sixth rule runs thus: 'Bibles in the vulgar tongue with all their parts are prohibited.' And in the recent index published by order of Pope Clement VIII, the faculty of granting license to read or keep vulgar Bibles or other parts of Sacred Scripture of both New and Old Testament, even when published in the vulgar tongue, has been taken away." Thomas Harding against Jewel, Article 15 section 2 (in John Jewel volume 1 p. 120) holds the same with others; René Benoist of Angers, Biblical Miscellanies book 3 p. 177; Johannes Bunderius in his Compendium of theological matters title 3 article 3; Johannes Molanus of Louvain in his Compendium of practical theology treatise 3 chapter 23 conclusion 2 p. 221.

5. That those err who believe Sacred Scriptures hung from the neck are endowed with various virtues against the world's dangers, diseases, and demons. Alfonso Salmerón does not dare simply to disapprove this custom of the Roman church (Commentary on Gospel history volume 4 part 3 treatise 42), nor Martin Del Rio (Disquisitions on magic book 1 chapter 4 question 4), Juan Maldonado on John 6, Vitus Miletus in Discussion of 600 errors pp. 51–52, or Landulf the Carthusian in Meditations on the life of Christ part 2 chapter 63: "The word CONSUMMATUM," he says, "is reported by the experienced to be of great efficacy in dangers. And it is said to avail specially against an immoderate flow of blood from the nostrils, if with the same blood the same word is written on the patient's forehead." Other examples of pontifical superstition Johannes Weyer noted in On the illusions of demons book 5 chapter 4, and Martin Del Rio in Disquisitions on magic book 3 part 2 question 4 section 9. Refer here also the Enchiridion or Manual in which are found a devout prayer of Pope Leo, likewise some prayers against all the world's dangers, and a prayer of blessed Augustine and Cyprian, published at Venice by Thomas Membruni — from which it will be clearly seen how maliciously the pontifical Roman church abuses Scripture's words unto superstition and magic.

source_text: V. A ratione instrumenti movendi ac dirigendi. Nam nullum instrumentum agit, nisi a causa principe prius motum & ad agendum applicatum. Jam vero sacra Scriptura est instrumentum, illuminatio vero Spiritus sancti causa princeps aperti sensus Scripturae, Job 32.v.8. Sap. 7.v.21. & cap. 8.v.1. 2. Cor. 3.v.6. Act. 16.v.14. & cap. 26.v.18. Deut. 29.v.4. psal. 119.v.34. Eph. 4.v.23. Jer. 31.v.18. Ergo. VI. A materia precum. Nam quicquid filii Dei petunt, ut a Deo impetrent, ad consequendum salutarem, vivum & interiorem Scripturae sensum, id consecutionem istius sensus ordine naturae praecedit. Jam vero petunt illuminationem Spiritus sancti ad consequendum Scripturae sensum, psal. 119.v.18. Col. 4.v.3. Confer etiam veterem hymnum, Purifica oculum interioris hominis &c. & praefationem, quam Lutherus tomo 1. Germanico anno 1539 praemisit. Ergo nullum vivum sensum Scripturae consequi possumus, sine praevia Spiritus sancti illuminatione. VII. A ratione ἀδυναμίας nostrae. Nam si homo a natura nullis viribus verbum Dei, quod illi sensum suum proponit, interius affirmare & efficaciter velle potest, quod proprie juxta Scripturae phrasin est illud recte intelligere: omnino hanc efficacem & interiorem affirmationem illuminatio Spiritus sancti ordine naturae, licet tempore sint simul, praecedere oportet. Atqui verum est prius, Joh. 15.v.5. Nihil sine me potestis, & 1. Cor. 12.v.3. Nemo potest Jesum Dominum appellare sine Spiritu sancto. adde Phil. 2.v.13. Act. 16.v.14. Ergo & posterius. VIII. A ratione originis primae. Nam unde sensus Scripturae principium suum habet, inde etiam cognoscitur. Quod enim est causa causae, id etiam est causa causati. Unde Bernhardus sermone ad fratres in monte: Nunquam, inquit, sensum Pauli ingredieris, nisi Pauli spiritum imbiberis. Et priscorum non nemo alius: Nemo Deum invenire potest, nisi prior a Deo inventus sit. Sic Didymus de Spiritu sancto: Nunquam, inquit, accipit quisquam spirituales benedictiones, nisi praecesserit Spiritus sanctus. Atqui sensus Scripturae principium suum habet ab illuminatione Spiritus sancti, 2. Pet. 1. & 2. Tim. 3. ult. Ergo &c.
english: V. From the reason of the instrument that moves and directs. For no instrument acts unless first moved by the principal cause and applied to acting. But now Sacred Scripture is an instrument, and the Holy Spirit's illumination is the principal cause of Scripture's opened sense ([[Job 32:8 >> Bible:Job 32:8]]; Wisdom 7:21 and chapter 8:1; [[2 Corinthians 3:6 >> Bible:2 Corinthians 3:6]]; [[Acts 16:14 >> Bible:Acts 16:14]] and [[Acts 26:18 >> Bible:Acts 26:18]]; [[Deuteronomy 29:4 >> Bible:Deuteronomy 29:4]]; [[Psalm 119:34 >> Bible:Psalm 119:34]]; [[Ephesians 4:23 >> Bible:Ephesians 4:23]]; [[Jeremiah 31:18 >> Bible:Jeremiah 31:18]]). Therefore.

VI. From the matter of prayers. For whatever the sons of God ask in order to obtain from God the salutary, living, and inward sense of Scripture precedes by nature the obtaining of that sense. But now they ask the Holy Spirit's illumination in order to obtain Scripture's sense ([[Psalm 119:18 >> Bible:Psalm 119:18]]; [[Colossians 4:3 >> Bible:Colossians 4:3]]). Compare also the old hymn "Purify the eye of the inward man," &c., and the preface which Luther prefixed to German volume 1 in the year 1539. Therefore we can obtain no living sense of Scripture without the Holy Spirit's prior illumination.

VII. From the reason of our inability. For if by nature a person with no powers can inwardly affirm and effectually will God's word, which proposes its sense to him — which properly, according to Scripture's phrase, is to understand it rightly — then altogether the Holy Spirit's illumination must precede this effectual and inward affirmation in the order of nature, even though they are simultaneous in time. But the former is true ([[John 15:5 >> Bible:John 15:5]]: "You can do nothing without me"; and [[1 Corinthians 12:3 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 12:3]]: "No one can call Jesus Lord without the Holy Spirit"; add [[Philippians 2:13 >> Bible:Philippians 2:13]]; [[Acts 16:14 >> Bible:Acts 16:14]]). Therefore so is the latter.

VIII. From the reason of first origin. For whence Scripture's sense has its principle, thence it is also known. For what is the cause of a cause is also the cause of what is caused. Whence Bernard in a sermon to the brothers on the mount: "You will never," he says, "enter Paul's sense unless you have drunk in Paul's spirit." And not a few of the ancients otherwise: "No one can find God unless he has first been found by God." So Didymus On the Holy Spirit: "No one," he says, "ever receives spiritual blessings unless the Holy Spirit has gone before." But Scripture's sense has its principle from the Holy Spirit's illumination ([[2 Peter 1:20 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:20]]–[[2 Peter 1:21 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:21]]; [[2 Timothy 3:16 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:16]]–[[2 Timothy 3:17 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:17]]). Therefore, &c.

source_text: II. Ex dictis inferimus, 1. Lectionem sacrae Scripturae non solum ecclesiasticis, sed & politicis, adeoque iis, quos in papatu Laicos vocant, ad salutem & spirituum discretionem longe utilissimam esse, agnoscente id Claudio Espencaeo comment. ad 1. Tit. cap. 1. & 2. Merito, inquit, omnes hortatur Chrysostomus ad Scripturarum lectionem: Voluit Deus, ut opifex omnium indoctissimus aliquid utilitatis reportaret. Quod studium divinitus approbatur psal. 1.v.2. & 119.v.2. & Act. 17.v.11. ideoque prophetae & Apostoli libros suos non solis doctoribus, sed toti ecclesiae commendârunt, Deut. 17.v.18. Rom. 1.v.7. 1. Cor. 1. 1. Pet. 1.v.1. 1. Joh. 2.v.12.13. Unde rursum Espencaeus in 2. Tim. 3. Origenes, inquit, observet, Johannem quatuor aetatibus scribere: pueris, adolescentibus, juvenibus, patribus.
english: II. From what has been said we infer:

1. That the reading of Sacred Scripture is by far most useful unto salvation and the discerning of spirits not only for ecclesiastics but also for those in civil life, and so even for those whom the papacy calls laity — Claude d'Espence acknowledging this in his commentary on 1 Timothy chapters 1 and 2: "Chrysostom," he says, "rightly exhorts all to the reading of the Scriptures: God willed that even the most unlearned craftsman of all should gain some usefulness." That study is approved from heaven ([[Psalm 1:2 >> Bible:Psalm 1:2]]; [[Psalm 119:2 >> Bible:Psalm 119:2]]; [[Acts 17:11 >> Bible:Acts 17:11]]); and therefore the prophets and Apostles recommended their books not to teachers alone but to the whole church ([[Deuteronomy 17:18 >> Bible:Deuteronomy 17:18]]; [[Romans 1:7 >> Bible:Romans 1:7]]; 1 Corinthians 1; [[1 Peter 1:1 >> Bible:1 Peter 1:1]]; [[1 John 2:12 >> Bible:1 John 2:12]]–[[1 John 2:13 >> Bible:1 John 2:13]]). Whence again d'Espence on 2 Timothy 3: "Let Origen," he says, "observe that John writes to four ages: children, youths, young men, fathers."

source_text: IX. Ab heterodidascalia. Nam quae doctrina proprie Photinianorum error est, ea in Ecclesia Dei tolerari non debet. Atqui Scripturam sine praevia Spiritus sancti illuminatione salutariter intelligi posse, Photinianorum error est. Nam Christophorus Ostorodius in institutione Germanica c. 1. §. 3. Nos, inquit, judicamus, omnes eos graviter admodum & periculose errare, qui opinantur, sacram Scripturam sine praevia interiore illuminatione & singulari revelatione S.S. fidem & obedientiam nullo modo operari posse. Quoniam vero haec Photinianorum doctrina falsa est, utique ejus contradictoria, quam hic defendimus, vera est. Manet igitur, etsi sacra Scriptura lumen grammaticum & lucem historicam sine singulari illuminatione Spiritus sancti spargat & communicet, quam etiam daemones & impii videre possunt: tamen interiorem & vivam notitiam in Scriptura neminem animo suo concipere posse, nisi illuminans, influens, disponens, cooperans, elevans lumen gratiae, tanquam causa princeps, praecedat, comitetur & subsequatur. X. A testimonio & consensu piae antiquitatis contra Pelagianos, qui nullum aliud lumen, quam grammaticum sive historicum, adeoque suasione morali duntaxat, hominem convertens agnoverunt. Contra quos vide Augustinum de fide ad Petrum, c. 32. Firmissime, inquit, tene & nullatenus dubites, posse quidem hominem, quem nec ignorantia literarum, nec aliqua prohibet imbecillitas vel adversitas, verba sanae legis & Euangelii sive legere, sive ex ore cujusdam praedicatoris audire: sed ut, quod audit corpore, etiam corde percipiat, & mandata Dei facere velit, nemo potest, nisi quem Deus gratia sua praevenerit, data divinitus bona voluntate & virtute. Sic Prosper Aquitanicus de ingratis: Percurrat, inquit, Apostolus orbem, praedicet, hortetur, plantet, riget, increpet, insistat, quamcumque viam verbo reclusam invenerit intret: ut tamen his studiis auditor promoveatur, non doctor, non discipulus, sed sola gratia efficit, non quae concilio tantum hortatuque benigno suadet, sed & mutat mentes, intusque reformat, vasque novum ex fracto fingit virtute creandi.
english: IX. From false teaching. For a doctrine that is properly the Photinians' error ought not to be tolerated in God's church. But that Scripture can be understood salutarily without the Holy Spirit's prior illumination is the Photinians' error. For Christoph Ostorodt in his German Institution chapter 1 §3 says: "We judge that all those err most gravely and dangerously who think Sacred Scripture can in no way work faith and obedience without prior inward illumination and a singular revelation of the Holy Spirit." But since this Photinian doctrine is false, its contradictory — which we here defend — is certainly true. It remains, therefore, that although Sacred Scripture scatters and communicates a grammatical light and historical light without the Holy Spirit's singular illumination — which even demons and the ungodly can see — yet no one can conceive in his mind an inward and living knowledge in Scripture unless the illuminating, influencing, disposing, cooperating, elevating light of grace, as principal cause, goes before, accompanies, and follows.

X. From the testimony and consent of pious antiquity against the Pelagians, who acknowledged no other light converting a person than the grammatical or historical, and so by moral persuasion only. Against them see Augustine, On faith to Peter, chapter 32: "Hold most firmly," he says, "and doubt in no way, that a person whom neither ignorance of letters nor any weakness or adversity hinders can indeed read the words of the sound law and Gospel, or hear them from some preacher's mouth: but that what he hears with the body he also perceives with the heart, and wills to do God's commandments — no one can, unless God has gone before him with his grace, a good will and power having been given from heaven." So Prosper of Aquitaine, Against the ungrateful: "Let the Apostle," he says, "run through the world, preach, exhort, plant, water, rebuke, insist, enter whatever way he finds closed by the word: yet that the hearer is advanced by these labors is effected not by the teacher, not by the disciple, but by grace alone — grace that does not merely counsel by kindly advice and exhortation, but also changes minds, reforms inwardly, and by creating power fashions a new vessel from a broken one."
